lesson.menu_title: The Mandate — Telling the Story of a Job You Were Given
lesson.menu_desc: What you were hired to do, what you inherited, and what you would have done differently -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- The Mandate: Telling the Story of a Job You Were Given
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 2 -- The Mandate

listenings.text: Fernando, Claire again. I have the debrief from the panel and I want you to hear it before we talk. They liked the numbers, and they said so twice. What they wrote down, and I am reading it to you, is that they never quite understood what you were actually hired to do in that group. Which surprised me, because you told me in five seconds. So here is what I want for the second round. Open with the mandate. One sentence. What the group asked you to deliver when you walked in, and what shape the finance function was in when you got there. Then the numbers. Not the other way round. And one more thing they flagged. When they asked what you would have done differently, you gave them a very careful answer and it sounded like you were protecting somebody. Give them a real one next time. Nobody trusts a CFO who has never changed his mind.

The honest answer is that I inherited a mess and I did not say so for eight months. My remit was to bring the reporting line under control, and the headcount I had was about a third of what the job needed. If I had asked for the backing in month one, I think I would have got it. I waited until I had the full picture, because that is how I am built, and by the time I asked, the year was gone and the board had stopped listening. With hindsight, that was the turning point of my whole tenure there, and I missed it. The lesson I took, and I have applied it since, is that you buy credibility by being early and wrong far more cheaply than by being late and right. If I could go back, that is the only thing I would change. Everything else I would do exactly the same way.

reading.rtitle: What a search firm actually writes down about you
paras: Every executive search firm keeps a candidate note, and it is shorter than candidates imagine. Two or three paragraphs, written within an hour of the interview, and read by people who will never meet you. The note almost never says that someone lacked technical depth. At CFO level that is assumed, and it was tested long before the interview.

What the note says, again and again, is that the panel could not work out what the candidate had been hired to do. A finance director will describe eleven years of results and never once state the mandate. The panel is left holding a list of achievements with no job attached to them, and a list is not a story.

The strongest candidates open the other way round. They give the remit in one sentence, describe the state of the function they inherited, and only then bring the numbers. A tenure told that way explains itself: the reader knows what good looked like before the first figure appears.

The second thing the note records is what the candidate would have done differently. Panels do not ask this to find a weakness. They ask it because a leader who has never revised a decision has either not made enough of them or is not telling the truth. The answer that works names one real turning point, says what the alternative was, and stops. The answer that fails is the one that protects everybody and commits to nothing.
reading.source: Adapted from executive search practice notes

choices: Search firms reject CFO candidates mainly for weak technical knowledge.
Panels remember the mandate and the revised decision, not the list of results.
Candidate notes are long, detailed documents written weeks after the interview.
